title: Ginataang tulingan
intro: Bullet tuna slowly simmered with kamias and ginger until tender, then finished in coconut milk with long green chilies. The fish is dense and rich, and the sauce is creamy with a sour edge.

items.name: tulingan
items.note: bullet tuna, 4 to 5 fish, gutted, gills removed, halved crosswise

items.name: kamias
items.note: bilimbi, halved, or 3 tbsp cane vinegar

steps.text: Rinse the fish well, rub with the salt and pack the pieces snugly in a pot.
Tuck the kamias, ginger, garlic, onion and peppercorns around the fish and pour in the water.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat without stirring until the fish is firm and most of the liquid is gone. Shake the pot now and then.
Pour in the coconut milk and add the chilies. Simmer uncovered, spooning sauce over the fish, until slightly reduced.
Add the coconut cream and simmer until the sauce is thick and the oil starts to separate. Taste, adjust the salt and serve with rice.

tips: Like most slow-cooked fish dishes, this tastes better the next day. Reheat it gently without stirring so the fish stays whole.

title: Ginataang sigarilyas
intro: Winged beans and pork simmered in coconut milk with shrimp paste and chili. The beans stay crunchy and grassy against the rich, salty sauce.

items.name: sigarilyas
items.note: winged beans, ends trimmed, sliced diagonally

steps.text: Put the pork in a pan over medium heat and cook until it renders some fat and turns golden.
Add the onion, garlic and ginger and cook until soft. Stir in the shrimp paste and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until the pork is tender and the sauce reduces a little.
Add the winged beans, chilies and coconut cream. Simmer until the beans are tender-crisp and still green.
Season with pepper, taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Winged beans go dull and soft quickly, so add them last and take the pan off the heat while they still snap.

title: Gising-gising
intro: Finely chopped string beans and ground pork cooked in coconut milk with plenty of chili. It is crunchy, creamy and spicy enough to wake you up.

items.name: sitaw
items.note: string beans, chopped into 5 mm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the ground pork and cook, breaking it up, until no longer pink and starting to brown. Add the fish sauce and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until reduced by about a third.
Add the string beans, chilies and coconut cream. Simmer, stirring, until the beans are tender-crisp and the sauce is thick.
Season with pepper and more fish sauce to taste. Serve with rice.

tips: Winged beans (sigarilyas) chopped the same way are the other common choice. Chop the beans small and evenly so they cook in a few minutes.

title: Ginataang gulay
intro: A mix of garden vegetables simmered in coconut milk seasoned with shrimp paste: squash, string beans, eggplant and okra. It is creamy and savory, a good way to use up whatever is in the crisper.

items.name: sitaw
items.note: string beans, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft and fragrant.
Stir in the shrimp paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the coconut milk and squash. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the squash is almost tender.
Add the string beans and eggplant and simmer until the eggplant softens.
Add the okra, chilies and coconut cream and simmer until the okra is just tender.
Taste and add a little more shrimp paste or salt if needed. Serve with rice.

tips: Add the vegetables in order of how long they take, hardest first, so nothing turns to mush.

title: Ginataang ampalaya
intro: Sliced bitter gourd and shrimp simmered in coconut milk. The creamy sauce softens the bitterness, leaving a pleasant, mellow bite.

items.name: medium ampalaya
items.note: bitter gourd, halved, seeded and thinly sliced

steps.text: Rub the bitter gourd slices with the salt and leave them for 15 minutes. Squeeze out the liquid, rinse and squeeze dry.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and tomato until the tomato softens.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce and simmer until slightly reduced.
Add the bitter gourd and chili and simmer without stirring until the gourd is tender but still green.
Add the shrimp and simmer until pink. Taste, adjust the fish sauce and serve with rice.

tips: For less bitterness, scrape out all the white pith with the seeds and salt the slices well. Leave them unstirred until cooked so they stay whole.

title: Sinantol
intro: Grated santol rind simmered in coconut milk with pork, shrimp paste and chili until soft and thick. It tastes sour, creamy and spicy, a little like laing with a citrusy tang.

steps.text: Peel the santol thinly and discard the skin. Grate the thick white rind on the coarse side of a grater down to the seeds; keep the pulp and seeds to eat as fruit.
Toss the grated rind with the salt, then squeeze it hard by the handful to remove the sour, astringent juice. Rinse once and squeeze dry. You should have about 4 cups.
Put the pork in a wide pot over medium heat and cook until it renders some fat and turns golden.
Add the onion, garlic and ginger and cook until soft. Stir in the shrimp paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the grated santol and the coconut milk. Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until the santol is soft and most of the liquid is absorbed.
Add the coconut cream and all the chilies. Simmer, stirring often so it does not catch, until very thick and the oil starts to separate.
Taste and add a little salt only if needed. Serve with rice.

tips: Use firm, just-ripe santol: overripe fruit has a thin rind and less to grate. Sinantol keeps for 4 days in the fridge.

title: Ginataang tahong
intro: Fresh mussels steamed open in coconut milk with lemongrass, ginger and long green chilies. The mussel juices mix with the coconut to make a sweet, briny sauce.

steps.text: Discard any mussels that are cracked or stay open when tapped.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft and fragrant.
Add the lemongrass, coconut milk and fish sauce and bring to a simmer.
Add the mussels and chilies, cover and cook, shaking the pot once or twice, until the shells open.
Discard any mussels that stay closed. Season the sauce with pepper and more fish sauce to taste, and serve with rice.

tips: Mussels release a lot of salty liquid, so taste the sauce before adding more fish sauce.

title: Ginataang pusit
intro: Tender squid rings cooked quickly in a thick, gingery coconut sauce with long green chilies. It is sweet, creamy and mild, without the vinegar and soy sauce of adobo.

items.name: small squid
items.note: cleaned, ink sacs removed, bodies cut into rings

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic, ginger and tomato until the tomato softens.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce and simmer until reduced by about a third.
Add the coconut cream and chilies and simmer until thick.
Add the squid and cook, stirring, just until it turns opaque and curls. Take the pan off the heat right away.
Taste, adjust the fish sauce and serve with rice.

tips: Squid turns rubbery after a few minutes and only softens again after half an hour, so cook it briefly in a sauce that is already thick.

title: Ginataang halaan
intro: Clams cooked in coconut milk with ginger and a handful of malunggay leaves. It is light, briny and creamy, with a sauce made for spooning over rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft and fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the clams and chilies, cover and cook, shaking the pot now and then, until the shells open.
Discard any clams that stay closed. Stir in the malunggay and cook just until wilted.
Taste the sauce and add fish sauce only if needed. Serve with rice.

tips: To purge clams, soak them in salted water for 1 to 2 hours and lift them out so the sand stays behind.

title: Piaparan a manok
intro: Chicken cooked with grated coconut, coconut milk, turmeric, lemongrass, ginger and chili until the sauce is thick, yellow and fragrant. The grated coconut gives it body and a nutty, gently sweet taste.

items.name: lemongrass stalks
items.note: bruised and tied in a knot

items.name: palapa
items.note: optional; or 2 scallions plus 1 more chili, chopped

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the shallots, garlic, ginger and turmeric until soft and fragrant.
Add the chicken and salt and stir to coat the pieces. Cook until the chicken is no longer pink outside.
Add the lemongrass, grated coconut and coconut milk. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender.
Stir in the palapa (or scallions) and the chilies. Simmer uncovered, stirring often so the coconut does not catch, until the sauce is thick and clings to the chicken.
Remove the lemongrass, taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Palapa is a relish of sakurab (a mild scallion), ginger and chili sold in jars; a spoonful of it adds a sharp, toasty flavor. Scallions and chili are a fine stand-in.

title: Piaparan a ikan
intro: Firm fish simmered with grated coconut, coconut milk, turmeric, ginger and lemongrass until the sauce is thick and golden. It is fragrant, nutty and gently spicy.

items.name: firm fish
items.note: tilapia, tanigue or maya-maya, cut into serving pieces

items.name: lemongrass stalks
items.note: bruised and tied in a knot

items.name: palapa
items.note: optional; or 2 scallions plus 1 more chili, chopped

steps.text: Rub the fish with the salt and set aside while you start the sauce.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the shallots, garlic, ginger and turmeric until soft and fragrant.
Add the lemongrass, grated coconut and coconut milk. Simmer, stirring now and then, until slightly thickened.
Lay the fish in the sauce in a single layer. Simmer uncovered, spooning sauce over the top instead of stirring, until the fish is cooked through.
Add the palapa (or scallions) and chilies and simmer until the sauce is thick. Remove the lemongrass, taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: Shake the pan gently instead of stirring once the fish is in, so the pieces stay whole.

title: Ginataang kangkong with dilis
intro: Water spinach wilted in coconut milk with garlic, chili and crisp-fried dried anchovies. It is a quick, cheap and savory vegetable ulam.

items.name: bunches kangkong
items.note: water spinach, about 500 g, stems and leaves separated, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Fry the dilis, stirring, until crisp and golden. Lift out half and set aside for topping.
In the same oil, cook the onion and garlic until soft.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until slightly reduced.
Add the kangkong stems and chili and simmer until the stems are tender-crisp.
Add the leaves and cook just until wilted. Season with pepper, and with fish sauce only if needed. Top with the reserved dilis and serve right away.

tips: Dilis are salty, so taste before adding fish sauce. Keep the topping portion separate until serving so it stays crisp.

title: Ginataang labong
intro: Strips of bamboo shoot simmered in coconut milk with shrimp and malunggay leaves. The shoots stay crunchy and slightly earthy in a mild, creamy sauce.

items.name: labong
items.note: boiled bamboo shoots, cut into thin strips

steps.text: Put the bamboo shoots in a pot of fresh water, bring to a boil and boil for 10 minutes to remove their strong smell. Drain and rinse.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft.
Add the bamboo shoots and fish sauce and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until the shoots are tender and the sauce reduces a little.
Add the shrimp and chilies and simmer until the shrimp turn pink.
Stir in the malunggay and cook until wilted. Taste, adjust the fish sauce and serve with rice.

tips: Fresh bamboo shoots must be peeled and boiled well before using; ready-boiled shoots sold in markets or packs still need the 10-minute boil here.

title: Ginataang upo
intro: Tender bottle gourd and shrimp simmered in coconut milk. It is soft, mild and lightly sweet, an easy everyday vegetable dish.

items.name: medium upo
items.note: bottle gourd, about 800 g, peeled, seeded and cut into thin strips

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and tomato until the tomato softens.
Add the shrimp and stir until they just turn pink. Lift them out and set aside.
Add the upo and fish sauce and cook, stirring, until it starts to release its water.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until the upo is soft and translucent.
Return the shrimp and simmer for 1 minute. Season with pepper and more fish sauce to taste. Serve with rice.

tips: Upo gives off a lot of water, so it needs less coconut milk than most ginataan; simmer uncovered if the sauce looks thin.

title: Ginataang gabi
intro: Taro and pork simmered in coconut milk with shrimp paste until the taro turns soft and thickens the sauce. It is starchy, creamy and savory, a hearty ulam for rice.

items.name: gabi
items.note: taro, peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks

steps.text: Wear gloves or oil your hands when peeling the taro, since the raw sap can itch. Rinse the chunks.
Put the pork in a pot over medium heat and cook until it renders some fat and turns golden.
Add the onion, garlic and ginger and cook until soft. Stir in the shrimp paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the taro and coconut milk. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, until the taro is tender when pierced. Stir gently now and then.
Add the coconut cream and chilies and simmer uncovered until the sauce is thick, mashing a few taro pieces into it.
Taste and add salt if needed. Serve with rice.

tips: Taro scorches easily once the sauce thickens; keep the heat low and scrape the bottom of the pot when you stir.

title: Ginataang sardinas
intro: Canned sardines in tomato sauce simmered with coconut milk and pechay. It is a fast pantry ulam with a creamy, tangy sauce.

items.name: pechay
items.note: bok choy, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until slightly reduced.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the chili. Simmer gently, without breaking up the fish too much.
Add the pechay and cook until just wilted. Season with pepper, taste and serve with rice.

tips: Canned sardines are already salted, so this rarely needs fish sauce. Misua noodles added with the pechay stretch it further.

title: Ginataang talong
intro: Pan-fried eggplant simmered with ground pork in coconut milk and shrimp paste. The eggplant turns silky and soaks up the rich, salty sauce.

items.name: long eggplants
items.note: about 500 g, sliced diagonally 1 cm thick

steps.text: Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Fry the eggplant in batches until lightly browned on both sides. Set aside.
Add the remaining oil and cook the onion, garlic and tomato until soft.
Add the ground pork and cook, breaking it up, until browned. Stir in the shrimp paste and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer until slightly reduced.
Return the eggplant, add the chilies and simmer until the eggplant is soft and the sauce is thick. Taste and serve with rice.

tips: Frying the eggplant first keeps it from turning grey and soggy in the sauce.

title: Ginataang bulaklak ng kalabasa
intro: Squash blossoms, string beans and shrimp cooked briefly in coconut milk. The flowers are tender and delicate, and the sauce is light, creamy and sweet.

items.name: squash blossoms
items.note: bulaklak ng kalabasa, stems peeled, stamens removed

items.name: sitaw
items.note: string beans, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Rinse the blossoms gently and shake dry. Leave them whole or tear large ones in half.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and garlic until soft.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce, add the string beans and simmer until the beans are almost tender.
Add the shrimp and simmer until they turn pink.
Lay the blossoms on top and simmer just until wilted, pressing them gently into the sauce. Season with pepper and more fish sauce to taste. Serve right away.

tips: Squash blossoms wilt within a day of picking, so cook them the day you buy them.

title: Ginataang dalag
intro: Mudfish simmered in coconut milk with ginger, mustard greens and long green chilies. The firm white fish stays meaty, and the greens add a peppery bite to the creamy sauce.

items.name: dalag
items.note: mudfish, cleaned and cut into 5 cm pieces

items.name: mustasa
items.note: mustard greens, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Rub the fish pieces all over with the coarse salt to remove the slime, then rinse well and pat dry.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and ginger until soft and fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce and bring to a gentle boil.
Add the fish in a single layer. Simmer uncovered, spooning sauce over the top instead of stirring, until the fish is cooked through.
Add the coconut cream, chilies and mustard greens and simmer until the greens are tender.
Taste, adjust the fish sauce and serve with rice.

tips: Ask the fish vendor to kill and clean the dalag for you. Pechay works if you cannot find mustasa.

title: Ginataang pako
intro: Young fiddlehead fern tips cooked quickly in coconut milk with shrimp and tomato. The ferns stay crisp and grassy in a light, creamy sauce.

items.name: bunches pako
items.note: fiddlehead fern, about 400 g, tender tops and leaves only

steps.text: Rinse the fern well and snap the stems into 5 cm pieces, discarding the tough lower parts.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic, ginger and tomatoes until the tomatoes soften.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce and simmer until slightly reduced.
Add the shrimp and simmer until they turn pink.
Add the fern and cook, tossing, just until bright green and wilted. Taste, adjust the fish sauce and serve right away.

tips: Pako cooks in a couple of minutes and turns slimy if overcooked, so add it last.

title: Sinanglay na tilapia
intro: Whole tilapia stuffed with tomato, onion and ginger, wrapped in pechay leaves and simmered in coconut milk with chilies. The fish stays moist inside its leaves, and the sauce is rich and gently spicy.

items.name: small tilapia
items.note: about 250 g each, cleaned and scaled

steps.text: Rub the fish inside and out with the salt. Mix the tomatoes, onion and minced ginger and stuff the bellies of the fish with it.
Dip the pechay leaves in boiling water for a few seconds to soften, then drain.
Wrap each fish in 3 or 4 leaves, leaving the head and tail out if you like. Tie loosely with kitchen string.
Lay the wrapped fish side by side in a wide pan. Pour the coconut milk over and add the sliced ginger, chilies, fish sauce and any leftover stuffing.
Bring to a gentle boil, then simmer uncovered over low heat, spooning sauce over the fish now and then. Do not turn the fish.
Pour in the coconut cream and simmer until the sauce thickens and the oil begins to separate.
Taste the sauce and adjust the fish sauce. Snip the strings and serve with the sauce and rice.

tips: Mustard leaves (mustasa) make a sharper-tasting wrapper if you prefer them to pechay.

title: Pyanggang manok
intro: Chicken simmered in coconut milk with a paste of deeply toasted coconut, lemongrass, ginger and chili. The paste turns the sauce dark brown and gives it a smoky, nutty taste.

steps.text: Toast the grated coconut in a dry wok or skillet over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until it is evenly very dark brown, almost black, and smells smoky. Do not let it burn to ash.

Grind the toasted coconut with the shallots, garlic, ginger, turmeric, lemongrass and chilies to a thick, dark paste in a food processor or mortar, adding a few spoonfuls of the coconut milk to help it along.
Rub the chicken all over with half of the paste and the salt.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and brown the chicken lightly on all sides.
Add the rest of the paste, the coconut milk and soy sauce. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender.
Uncover and simmer, stirring often so the bottom does not catch, until the sauce is thick and dark and coats the chicken. Taste and add the sugar and more salt if needed.
Serve with rice.

tips: Toasting the coconut evenly is the whole trick: keep the heat low and keep stirring, and pull it off a shade early if any bits start to smell acrid.
